eta.method: trend (log-linear fleet growth in the lead metro) with a mixture over denominator readings; Monte Carlo (N=200k) plus reference-class and proponent checks
eta.calc: Waymo rides/wk 250k (Apr 2025) -> 450k (Dec 2025) = 1.8x in 8 mo = 2.41x/yr; fleet ~2,500 in 6 cities (Dec 2025). Lead metro SF: Waymo ~1,000 (assumed ~40% of fleet, range 700-1,300; not in ledger). Denominator: broad (taxis + ride-hail on road at peak) ~6,000 (4k-12k; SFCTA background) weight 0.7 -> gap 6x; narrow (licensed taxis ~1,500) weight 0.3 -> gap 1.5x. Per-metro growth +55%/yr (30-100%; half of total log growth, fleet split over new metros). Broad: ln(6)/ln(1.55) = 4.1 yr after 2025.95 -> 2030.0 (+0.25-1.5 yr to a published count). MC: all p10 2027.7/p50 2030.0/p90 2033.5; broad 2028.9/2030.8/2034.2; narrow 2027.3/2028.0/2029.2. p90 widened to 2038 for a Cruise-type stall or strict L5 reading. Wuhan cross-check: Baidu 1,000+ vs ~10^4 taxis = >=10x -> later. Tesla's 2025 dates missed entirely (discounted). Prev v1 ETA '5-10 yrs (~2031-2036)'.
eta.cruxes: Earlier: a published per-city fleet count (CPUC/SFMTA/Waymo) with SF robotaxis >= licensed taxis, or Baidu/Pony fleet jumps in Wuhan/Shenzhen. Later: lead-metro fleet growth <30%/yr, a serious-incident shutdown, a ride-hail-inclusive denominator >10k, or a strict reading of '(L5)' (all deployments are geofenced L4).

eta.method: driver trend (exponential reliability growth, embodied doubling tied to METR horizons) plus a disclosure lag; Monte Carlo (N=200k); discounted-proponent and reference-class checks
eta.calc: Gap = interventions/shift I0 vs <=1. 84 s cycle -> 8*3600/84 = 343 cycles/shift; ~2% per-cycle failure (pi0.5 88-100% on trained tasks) x ~35% not self-recovered (STAR 78% lab recovery) = 2.4/shift, x2 for non-cycle failures -> I0 ~5 (1.5-30) = 2.3 doublings. Driver (robots-software, series metr-80-horizon-by-release --as-of 2026-10-06): p80 frontier 4.42 min (2024-09-12) -> 185.91 min (2026-04-07), 42x, 4.45-mo doubling (long run 6.4 mo); embodied doubling T_e assumed 11 mo (80% range 7-18) since VLA reliability lags software agents (REALM, VLA-survey events). Capability = 2025.9 + log2(5) x 11/12 = 2028.0; + disclosure lag median 1 yr (0.3-3). MC: capability p50 2027.9; ETA p10 2027.1/p50 2029.3/p90 2032.8; P(<=2031.76) = 0.83. p90 widened to 2034. label: Progressing: humanoids staff 1 station on day shifts; 24/7 robot-only line ~5 doublings, ETA ~2035
rationale: No event shows a multi-station line run only by general-purpose robots; the precursors are single-station humanoids on supervised 10-hour day shifts (Figure/BMW) and Digit's autonomous docking at GXO. A 10-robot line running 168 h with no humans needs about 30x the Blue Collar reliability (~4.9 doublings beyond it), plus robot-performed maintenance and a software changeover. Chaining that onto the Blue Collar capability (~2028) at an 11-month embodied doubling, plus ~1.5 yr of staging, gives ~2035 (80% range 2031-2046). The median is within 10 years and the drivers measurably move, so it is yellow; it sits near the 10-year line.

basis.rule: Milestone yellow (RUBRIC v2 §4): measurable progress on drivers the milestone is tied to (single-station full-shift humanoid deployments, autonomous docking, the autonomy trend), median ETA 2035 <= made_at + 10 yr; not green (median > 5 yr, no multi-station precursor)

eta.method: driver trend (exponential reliability growth chained from the Blue Collar capability) plus a staging lag; Monte Carlo (N=200k); reference-class check
eta.calc: ~10 robots (5 stations + movers + spares) x 168 h = 1,680 robot-h with no humans; 50% run success needs MTB-unrecoverable >= 1,680/ln2 = 2,424 robot-h; if peers/spares absorb 90% of interventions, Blue-Collar-sense MTBI >= 242 h vs 8 h = 30x = 4.9 doublings (97% absorbed: 3.2; 70%: 6.5). Driver (robots-software, series metr-80-horizon-by-release --as-of 2026-10-06): p80 frontier 4.42 min (2024-09-12) -> 185.91 min (2026-04-07), 42x, 4.45-mo doubling (long run 6.4 mo); embodied doubling T_e assumed 11 mo (80% range 7-18) since VLA reliability lags software agents (REALM, VLA-survey events). ETA = Blue Collar capability (2025.9 + log2(5) x 11/12 = 2028.0) + 4.9 x 11/12 (4.5 yr) + staging 1.5 yr (0.5-4) = 2034.0. MC: p10 2030.9/p50 2034.6/p90 2040.6; P(<=2036.76) = 0.71. p90 widened to 2046 (trend stall, or no one stages a humanoid-only line). Reference class: purpose-built robots took ~40 yr from Unimate (1961) to lights-out lines (~2001). Prev v1 ETA '>10 years (no evidenced path)'.
eta.cruxes: Earlier: a Blue Collar-grade disclosure (<=1 intervention/shift) by ~2028; >=10 humanoids on one line at one site; robot-performed battery swaps or maintenance in production; a staged multi-robot line demo (UBTech, Tesla, Figure). Later: intervention rates stuck >>1/shift, single-site fleets staying at <=5 units, humanoid programmes scaled back, or an embodied doubling time of >=15 months (pushes the median past 2036).

basis.path: Precursors: Figure 02 at BMW (one station, 10h shifts, support staff; Figure 03 successor); Digit at GXO (tote moves, ~4 h/battery, autonomous docking = self-charging precursor); UBTech Walker S2 500+ contracted for BYD/VW/Audi plants; Hyundai's planned Atlas deployment. label: Inching: touch sensors now common on robot hands; autonomous hands still lag teleoperated ones
rationale: Robot hands improved in small steps over the past year: hand makers say touch sensors went from about one in ten hands sold in China to most of them, in March a UT Austin two-finger gripper picked up raspberries and potato chips 92% of the time and caught slips, and companies reported their robots plugging wires into a moving target almost without fail and driving screws up to three times faster than before. None of this is close to a human hand: at the first dexterous-hand contest, at Beijing's World Humanoid Robot Games in August, remotely operated hands took at least five of the eight gold medals and only one was reported won fully autonomously; mainstream hands still do not last as long as real deployments need, and in September Tesla's hand assembly and unreliable touch sensors were reported to be holding back its Optimus production. Next to watch are the new touch-sensing hands from 1X, Sharpa and Boston Dynamics now going onto robots, and the replaceable sensing glove Tesla plans for next year's model.

label: Advancing: a robot folds laundry 99% right in unseen homes; most new tasks still fail often
rationale: In July Sunday Robotics reported its home robot folding laundry successfully 99% of the time over 785 tries in homes it had never seen, a reliability not reported before for a household chore in unfamiliar homes; in August Skild AI showed a model picking up unfamiliar several-minute tasks from a single video, two-thirds of their steps succeeding (scored step by step, with people stepping in to recover failed steps) against under a tenth for a comparable model given written instructions instead, and in September Figure reported its humanoid finishing chores in 30 unseen homes 56% of the time. These are the companies' own tests, and outside them robots still stumble when objects or rooms change slightly and often cannot recover from a first small mistake, as seen at Beijing's World Humanoid Robot Games in August, while Tesla's Optimus reportedly still takes days to learn basic tasks. Next to watch are NVIDIA's GR00T N2 model, due by the end of 2026, and whether Sunday's coffee-making and other skills reach its laundry standard.

label: Advancing: a four-legged robot ran a marathon on one charge; humanoids still last only 2-4 hours
rationale: In September a Nature paper reported that KAIST's four-legged robot had run a full marathon on a single battery charge in late 2024, using less energy per kilogram and kilometre than a human runner and going more than three times as far per charge as other four-legged robots; the robot has no arms, and whether its methods carry over to humanoids is untested. Humanoids got cheaper to make, with the average cost of a Unitree or Leju humanoid down about a quarter in 2025, but still run only 2-4 hours per charge, so full shifts rely on battery swaps or charging rotations, and better batteries are slow to arrive: XPeng reportedly had to settle for semi-solid cells in its humanoid because suppliers could not deliver suitable all-solid-state ones. Next to watch are Agility's Digit 5, promising 90 minutes of work per 9-minute charge, with early customers in the first half of 2027, and Samsung SDI's solid-state batteries, targeted for mass production in the second half of 2027.

World Humanoid Robot Games scenario events (reporters on site): nearly all full completions of packing and cable tasks were teleoperated; autonomous robots could not adjust after a first small error, and softer cables than in training made the task harder

Electrek/The Information: Tesla's Optimus AI reportedly cannot reliably handle a wide range of tasks, behaves unpredictably outside training and takes days to learn basic tasks despite 500k+ hours of data; factory units confined to programmed tasks

MarketWatch: Tau Robotics' paid in-home cleaning humanoids (~100 cleanings) were guided by remote operators in a reporter's apartment, struggled with a smooth glass and a small knife, and Tau says they are not fully autonomous: a commercial home service still depends on human takeover

basis.prospects: NVIDIA says GR00T N2, which it claims doubles success on new tasks in new environments, will be available at the end of 2026; Sunday says coffee-making and other household skills are not yet reliable enough to test against its laundry standard. Watch for outside measurements of whole-task success in unseen homes (Figure reports 56% for its own robot), of learning a task from one video (Skild reports two-thirds of steps succeeding, with people recovering failed steps), and for robots recovering from mistakes without human help in public competitions.

label: Inching: humanoid unit costs fell about a quarter; full shifts still need charging or swaps
rationale: Humanoids got cheaper to make over the past year, with IPO filings showing the average cost of building a Unitree or Leju humanoid down about a quarter in 2025, but runtime has not followed: mainstream humanoids still run 2-4 hours per charge, so robots cover long shifts by taking turns at the charger, as a Figure fleet did through a 200-hour package-sorting run in May. Better batteries are slow to arrive: in September XPeng reportedly settled for semi-solid cells in its humanoid because suppliers could not deliver suitable all-solid-state ones. Next to watch are Agility's Digit 5, promising 90 minutes of work per 9-minute charge with early customers in the first half of 2027, and Samsung SDI's solid-state batteries, targeted for mass production in the second half of 2027.

Figure 03 fleet sorted 249,560 packages over a 200-hour unedited livestream (reported by Humanoids Daily, Interesting Engineering) by autonomously rotating robots through chargers on roughly 4-hour batteries: covers shifts by rotation, not longer runtime, at Figure's own facility

Galbot S1 (spec: up to 8 h continuous operation on CATL batteries) worked 7x24 on CATL production lines for over three months; company/partner claim, 8 h is a specification rather than a measured run, and battery maintenance arrangements are undisclosed

Unitree final IPO prospectus: 5,215 humanoids sold in 2025 at an average ¥166,400 (-36% vs 2024, mostly the cheaper G1 mix); implied average unit cost ~¥61,000 vs ~¥80,000 (-24%). Measured cost decline from a regulatory filing, a refinement rather than a step change
Leju Kuavo full-size humanoid (IPO prospectus): 577 units in 2025 vs 32 in 2024, average price -25.6% to ¥308,100 and unit cost -27.4%; measured, a refinement

setbacks.what: CnEVPost/Jipian Lab: XPeng switched its IRON humanoid from announced all-solid-state batteries to semi-solid pouch cells after BYD, Gotion, CALB and Eve could not supply all-solid-state products meeting its requirements, so the battery-breakthrough route is not ready for its end-2026 production
The Information: hand-assembled hands (100+ parts, rework after misaligned assembly) and suppliers hold back Tesla's Optimus V3 ramp toward its volume (cost) targets

basis.prospects: Agility's Digit 5 (90-minute battery, 9-minute charge, early access in the first half of 2027) and Samsung SDI's all-solid-state batteries (mass production targeted for the second half of 2027) are the next named tests of runtime; XPeng plans to mass-produce its IRON humanoid on semi-solid cells from the end of 2026. Watch for measured shift-length runtimes of humanoids at work, and whether the energy-saving design KAIST published this year for a four-legged marathon robot carries over to humanoids.

basis.change_note: Audit correction (2026-10-28-challenges, robots.md MAJOR colour/window finding): green (Advancing) -> yellow (Inching), permitted without new evidence by rule 8. The previous record's only substantive advance, KAIST RAIBO2 (Nature, 23 Sep 2026; cost of transport 0.25 vs human 0.37, >3x range per charge), reports a marathon run in November 2024: §7 dates a result by the claim when it is earlier than the event's date, and peer review is neither a new run nor a replication, so it is historical context (cited in evidence, not listed as an advance); the previous record's 'judged on its publication date' was the error. The event's ledger date (2026-09-23, the publication) still needs correcting by gather; this record cannot edit events. With RAIBO2 removed no substantive advance remains: measured cost cuts (Unitree implied unit cost ~¥80k -> ~¥61k, -24%; Leju unit cost -27.35%) are refinements; Figure's 200-hour rotating-fleet livestream (added, third-party reported) covers shifts by charging rotation on ~4 h batteries rather than longer runtime, and replaces Figure's February 24/7 HQ claim as the listed rotation advance (the latter kept as context). Added per the cross-section findings (setbacks and advances sought among all section events; year-only records not excluded for precision alone): Galbot S1's 7x24 CATL run with an 8 h battery spec, and Kepler K2's single-charge 8-hour trade-show livestream (year-only 2025, possibly before the window), both non-substantive. Agility's 65,000 operating hours moved to context: it is a cumulative durability figure over nearly three years, not a runtime or cost result of the window. Setbacks re-weighed after removing RAIBO2 (audit): XPeng's retreat from all-solid-state cells and Tesla's hand-assembly snags are single-firm supply and manufacturing problems that do not reverse the filed cost declines, so Inching rather than Setback. Level: mainstream humanoid runtime 2-4 h per charge (TrendForce Jan 2026, Securities Times Jul 2026); 36Kr (Oct 2026) gives 2-3 h for entry-level models (some one hour) and 6-8 h specifications for commercial/flagship ones, specs not demonstrated as working shifts; Digit at Schaeffler works two 4-hour stints with a recharge between). Label adopts the audit's suggestion; no event ids in prospects. No new events since the previous record (ledger intake ends 2026-10-19).
